title: The Allocation You Did Not See: Count It, Do Not Time It

questions.question: A loop body that touches only stack was timed a hundred thousand times: median 0.250 us, worst 60.376 us. What does the worst case measure?
options: The operating system: a scheduling event, a page fault, an interrupt
A hidden allocation in the body
The timer's own resolution
Cache misses on the stack buffer
questions.explanation: The body that allocates had a worst case of 36 us, lower than the body that cannot. No timing threshold separates an allocation from the machine being busy.

questions.question: How do you find out whether a loop allocates?
options: Count allocations and assert the count is zero, which is deterministic and identical on every toolchain
Time the loop and look for outliers
Run a profiler and look at the malloc column
Read the code carefully
questions.explanation: It is also a different question from a leak: a loop that allocates and frees a hundred blocks a tick leaks nothing, and the live-block counters come back to where they started.

questions.question: A vector<string> is reserved to 64 and refilled each tick with 20-character strings. How many allocations per tick?
options: 64: reserve made room for 64 string objects, and each then went to the heap for its characters
0, since the vector was reserved
1, for the vector's buffer
13, from the vector's growth
questions.explanation: The same loop with strings short enough to live inside the string object allocates nothing at all. reserve reserves the container, not the things inside it.

questions.question: Why does the lesson's test search for the small-string limit rather than assuming it?
options: It is 15 characters on two of the libraries this curriculum builds against and 22 on the third, so a loop that is allocation free on a laptop may not be on the robot
Because it changes with the string's contents
Because it depends on the optimisation level
Because the standard leaves it unspecified between runs
questions.explanation: std::function has a boundary of the same kind: a lambda capturing one double fits inside it everywhere, three doubles does not on every library.

questions.question: A fixed-capacity pool is asked for a slot and has none. What should it do?
options: Return nothing, count the refusal, and let the caller decide, because growing gives up the only property it had
Allocate one more slot, since running out is rare
Block until a slot is returned
Reuse the oldest slot in use
questions.explanation: It would grow at the worst possible moment, which is when the system is already late. The count of refusals is what tells you the pool was sized for last year's worst case.

questions.question: Why does releasing the same slot twice matter more than it looks?
options: The free list then holds one index twice, so two later callers are handed the same object and the damage appears somewhere else entirely
It leaks the slot permanently
It corrupts the heap
It only matters if the pool is nearly full
questions.explanation: Refusing it and counting it turns a bug that shows up as impossible data in another subsystem into a number at the place the mistake was made.
